claims.statement: `nora.domain.ports.PlatformAdapter` declares exactly `platform`, `resolve_identity`, `listen`, `send`, `react` and `health`, and deliberately has no `parse()`: a port-level parse would force every adapter to pretend its transport is dict-shaped, so parsers stay per-adapter and are tested against their own transport shape.

`PlatformAdapter.send`'s `mentions`, `styles` and `preview` are the only defaulted parameters on the send path, deliberately, so a platform without those concepts ignores them and every failure upstream degrades to the plain message rather than to a refusal, which also lets a new adapter satisfy the port on the day it is written.

`SendResult` is a record rather than a bool so a rate limit can carry a retry delay, and `ReactionResult` carries `supported` beside `ok` so "this platform has no reactions" stays distinguishable from "the reaction failed".

`react()` lives on the adapter port rather than a separate capability protocol, and `nora.engagement.stages.indicate` tolerates an adapter with no `react` attribute at all via `getattr`, counting it `unsupported` and never crashing on it.

`AdapterRegistry.from_config` builds each enabled platform inside its own `if platforms.<x>.enabled:` block and resolves that adapter's identity inline before registering it, raising `AdapterRegistryError` (re-raised as `StartupError` by composition) because R-12 admits a tag by testing membership in a resolved `PlatformIdentity.aliases`, so an adapter that cannot say who Nora is could let her trigger herself.

`AdapterRegistry` is a frozen lookup table built once at startup: it performs no I/O itself and stores adapters typed as the `PlatformAdapter` port, so a caller reading through it never needs to know which concrete adapter it got.

`AdapterRegistry.self_aliases()` is a union of every resolved identity's aliases and is what `MentionPolicy`/`ReplyToNoraPolicy` test, while R-12's self-tag check deliberately stays per-platform and reads `identity_for(message.platform)`; the overlapping bare-digit id spaces mean a cross-platform false positive could engage a turn that did not tag Nora but could never miss one or resolve a person to the wrong `person_id`.

Instagram is the single exception to fail-fast identity resolution: a failed `resolve_identity` degrades the adapter and registers it with no entry in the registry's `identities` mapping, and that omission is load-bearing because a placeholder identity would inject a placeholder value into the alias set the mention and reply-to policies test; the exception is explicitly not extended to WhatsApp.

A degraded Instagram adapter sends and reacts nothing without an HTTP call (a refusal that is not retryable, and `react` answers `supported=False`), never opens its event stream and never returns from `listen()`, logs one startup ERROR line, and reports `degraded=True` with the reason as `detail` from `health()`.

Instagram degradation has two independent sources: the startup half is latched until restart, while the runtime half tracks the listener's heartbeat-reported session state, so a session checkpointed after boot is reported degraded and one that recovers stops being reported degraded without a restart.

Signal resolves identity in two steps: an account derivation that is fatal (the configured override is load-bearing because signal-cli's HTTP surface exposes no route or RPC that reveals the pinned account) and a typed-identifier enrichment that never raises, publishing `nora_identity_aliases{platform}` on every path and incrementing `nora_identity_enrichment_degraded_total{platform,reason}` per failure while falling back to the primary alone.

Identity memoization differs by platform on purpose: Signal caches success-or-degraded alike so `/health` polls never re-hit the daemon, while Discord, WhatsApp and Instagram cache success only, because a half-paired bridge or a checkpointed bridge that answers 200 with a cached self block would otherwise produce an identity that reads as fully healthy while every send fails.

Discord's identity comes from one authenticated REST call that returns the bot's snowflake (the only identifier recorded) plus a display handle read off the same response; the username is never an identity because an owner can rename the application at any time.

WhatsApp's identity comes from one bridge call returning the bot's phone and, when reported, its lid, and a failure is a startup error rather than a counted partial answer because the bridge answers in one body or not at all.

Instagram's identity is read from the bridge's health route and refuses any session state that is not exactly `authenticated`, because a checkpointed bridge still answers 200 with a cached self block and an adapter resolving identity from it would register as healthy and then fail every send.

`AdapterHealth.degraded` is a third state rather than a spelling of `connected=False`: a disconnected adapter is expected to heal on its own, while a degraded one is present, registered and structurally unable to act until a human intervenes, and `detail` carries the stated reason.

Nora's `/health` publishes one entry per enabled platform with connected/degraded/detail/last-event-age and the resolved account, records a platform whose `health()` raised as disconnected rather than omitting it, and deliberately does not treat a degraded platform as Nora being unhealthy — a 503 would fail the container healthcheck and take the other platforms down with it.

`nora.app.source_health` records adapter health as five states per transition (`up`, `stale`, `degraded`, `down`, `unknown`) using the same 900-second staleness threshold the platform-silent alert fires on, so "every source was healthy for this interval" is a query and a raising `health()` reads as «could not check» rather than «down».

Adapter supervision is one task per platform with capped exponential backoff and a per-platform restart counter, so a failing `listen()` is scoped to its own platform's health instead of taking down the process or another platform; because a supervisor only backs off on exceptions, a `listen()` that returns becomes a hot loop, which is why Discord builds a fresh client per attempt and a degraded Instagram adapter blocks forever.

`MediaSource` is a port separate from `PlatformAdapter`, bound to one platform and required never to raise, because fetching bytes is not part of the send/receive/react lifecycle and `MediaBytes` must carry the difference between "could not fetch" and "fetched nothing"; `MediaSourceRegistry.for_platform` makes "this platform has no fetcher" a countable value instead of a wrong call.

WhatsApp records the fact of media with no platform handle and has no `MediaSource`, so the ingest media stage counts its attachments `not_supported`; the registry is built unconditionally for Signal, Discord and Instagram because a fetcher for a platform producing no messages costs nothing and gating it would make custody depend on two settings.

Each platform's media fetcher resolves a different handle: Signal fetches signal-cli's own attachment id over the JSON-RPC endpoint it already uses (avoiding a second mount of the daemon's filesystem), Discord derives sticker URLs from id and format and allowlists attachment hosts before opening a socket, and Instagram treats the event's signed CDN URL as the handle and allowlists hosts by leading-dot suffix.

Parse-and-drop happens inside each adapter's `listen()`, which calls its own parser and only forwards a non-`None` `NormalizedMessage` to `on_message`, so `nora.ingest` never receives a raw platform event.

All four parsers converge on one normalization contract in which mentions are a separate set of id forms, a quote is a pointer rather than a copy of the parent text, media records what the platform said without downloading, `message_id` carries the platform's own handle (empty on Signal), and a reaction or delete arrives as a `Touch` on a message rather than as a message row.

Discord's adapter builds a fresh, single-use client and listener per `listen()` attempt and serializes inbound events per channel with an `asyncio.Lock`, so an edit cannot be ingested concurrently with the new message it edits and be dropped as an orphan, without serializing unrelated channels.

A `summons` event from the instagram-bridge is handed to a `SummonsSink` and never reaches ingest, because it is not a room message; the ordinary message event the bridge sends beside it is the room's copy.

`build_dependencies` treats the adapter registry as a fatal ordered startup step, converting `AdapterRegistryError` into `StartupError`, and refuses to start a registry with no `signal` entry even though the registry itself tolerates zero enabled platforms, because the rest of the composition has no code path that runs without an adapter.

Three of the four transports hold their session out of process: signal-cli, the whatsapp-bridge and the instagram-bridge each run in their own container on a private network that publishes nothing, mounting their session state on a volume kept outside the directory Nora bind-mounts because she must not read transport credentials.

Each bridge's container healthcheck proves only that its HTTP layer serves and cannot prove the platform socket is alive; the instagram-bridge's health route answers success while a session is checkpointed on purpose, because a challenge is a normal operating state and restarting fixes nothing, so the real socket-death detector is Nora's per-platform last-event age.

The instagram-bridge's single public write is switch-gated rather than unconditionally enabled: it is off unless the deployment sets exactly `on`, is rate-capped and spaced before any platform call, and latches off across restarts once the platform answers with an action block.
Discord has no bridge: its bot token is resolved from an environment variable by the composition root and threaded to the adapter, so no session state exists on disk for that platform.

The port contract is verified as real rather than aspirational: `tests/contract/test_port_conformance.py` asserts that all four concrete adapters satisfy `PlatformAdapter`, including an Instagram adapter in its degraded state.

`tests/unit/test_instagram_degradation.py` pins the degradation contract end to end: a checkpointed bridge still lets the registry build, a degraded adapter neither sends nor reacts against a bridge that would accept, a degraded `listen()` never returns, and a session checkpointed after startup degrades the live adapter.

`own_handle()` is not on the adapter port: Discord caches it from the identity call and Instagram reads it live per call, and it is display text for presence only, never entering `PlatformIdentity` and therefore never becoming a mention id.
